text.content: There are two common answers. One approach uses a central coordinator that decides how work moves through the system. The other lets agents interact directly and adjust on the fly. These two styles are called orchestration and choreography, and the choice between them shapes how the whole workflow behaves.

text.content: In a choreographed multi-agent system, there is no central coordinator responsible for managing the workflow. Instead, each agent understands its own role and communicates directly with other agents when additional information or capabilities are needed. When a request enters the system, one agent begins processing it and decides which other agents should be involved. Those agents exchange information with one another, contribute their specialized expertise, and continue collaborating until the task is completed. The final result emerges from the collective work of the agents rather than being assembled by a central controller.

text.content: This approach can be highly flexible because agents can interact dynamically based on the needs of the task. It also avoids creating a single coordination bottleneck, which can improve scalability in larger systems. However, because decisions and communication are distributed across multiple agents, choreographed systems can be more difficult to monitor, debug, and understand than orchestrated systems.

text.content: Orchestration and choreography solve the same coordination problem in different ways. Orchestration puts a coordinator in the middle — predictable, easier to reason about, easier to debug — at the cost of a central point of complexity. Choreography lets agents interact directly — more flexible and resilient — at the cost of visibility into how the system behaves. For Cascadia's support flow, Sofia will start with orchestration in the next lessons; it is the pattern that fits when the specialists are known ahead of time and a coordinator can be trusted to route them.
